web_title: 4. The Regulatory Clock, Substitutes & Helium Supply
question: Which rules and supply chains decide how long this company's main products stay the main products?

epigraph.quote: Adopted in 2016, the Amendment commits countries to reducing HFC production and consumption with differentiated timelines for developed and developing nations.
epigraph.author: UNEP Ozone Secretariat, Kigali Amendment overview [17]

web_blocks.html: Refrigerant gas is regulated before it is sold. The rules that shape this company’s product mix are not set in a boardroom. They sit in an international treaty, and the treaty decides how fast the company’s main molecules must shrink. This chapter reads the treaty as a supply rule for this business, then tests the helium supply chain, which has its own limits.

web_blocks.title: The Montreal Protocol and the Kigali Amendment

web_blocks.html: The Montreal Protocol is the treaty that phased out the ozone-depleting gases. The Kigali Amendment extended the framework to hydrofluorocarbons, the HFCs that replaced the older gases. The UNEP summary puts it plainly: “Adopted in 2016, the Amendment commits countries to reducing HFC production and consumption with differentiated timelines for developed and developing nations.” [17] Developed countries began their reductions in 2019 [17]. HFCs do not deplete the ozone layer, but they are potent greenhouse gases, and that is why they now sit under a timetable.

web_blocks.title: Where India sits in the schedule

web_blocks.html: India is in Group 2 of the HFC annex, with Bahrain, Iran, Iraq, Kuwait, Oman, Pakistan, Qatar, Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates [16]. For Group 2 the base level is the average HFC consumption for 2024 to 2026 plus 65% of the HCFC baseline. The freeze takes effect on 1 January 2028 [16]. A freeze caps consumption at the base level, so the national ceiling is set by the years that are happening now.

The treaty summary does not say how India will share its national ceiling among companies, and the sources I checked do not say either. That allocation is the part of the rule that would matter most to this business, and it is the one thing I could not verify. Ask for it before you assume anything about the company’s refrigerant volume after 2028.

R-32 is an HFC. The FY25 annual report records a partnership with Daikin for HFC-32 sourcing [4]. So the company’s largest product, and the planned Bhilwara R-32 plant, both sit inside the freeze rather than outside it [2][9].

The company is hedging the rule with lower-warming molecules. It supplies HFO-1234yf to Indian auto makers [4]. Its HFO plant at Bhilwara is planned under a memorandum of understanding with the state, at about ₹200 crore with construction from 2027 [2]. The Mambattu plant blends HFO with the company’s own R-32, and management says it will replace HFO blends the company now imports [9].

The hedge is real, but it is a different business. HFO products have their own chemistry, customers and input chains, and the sources do not give margins for them separately. Management says the HFO plant will raise revenue, EBITDA and profit significantly once it runs [9]. Test that against the filings when they arrive, not against the call.

On the August call, management said the company’s R-32 imports were over 4,000 tons before it began making R-32 itself, and that its own requirement would be roughly 40 to 50% of production [9]. That is a spoken figure, and I did not find it in a filing. It matters because it shows how much of the company’s refrigerant volume depends on what it can make itself, which is the point of the Bhilwara plant.

web_blocks.title: What to watch in the next filings

web_blocks.html: Three things will tell you more than any call. First, the national allocation of the India ceiling, once it is public, because it decides how much refrigerant volume the company can sell after 2028. Second, the HFO plant’s capex and construction start in the annual report, because the two figures in the sources need to converge. Third, the helium volume in the quarterly results, because management’s 20% utilisation view is testable one quarter at a time.

Keep the dates and the numbers in one place as you read. A regulatory date tells you when a product line must change. A capex line tells you whether the company can change in time. A volume line tells you whether the new plant is earning. The three together are the test of whether the substitute story is a plan or only a slide.

External Learning Hub. Check the regulatory and helium figures yourself. The treaty pages, the USGS commodity summary and the company’s own filing index are all public. web_blocks.title: Helium: a supply chain built on other countries

web_blocks.html: The helium project is the company’s other new line, and its supply rests on partners rather than on owned resources. Liquid helium comes through Sharjah Oxygen Company in Dubai, which sources from RAS Gases & Oilfields in Qatar [1]. Helium is recovered as a by-product, so supply follows the producers’ output rather than the company’s demand [11].

The USGS summary gives United States helium import sources for 2021 to 2024: Canada 47%, Qatar 28%, Algeria 10%, China 5% and other sources 10% [21]. These are United States figures, not India’s, and the company’s own supply mix is not disclosed. They still show concentration in the global market, with a large share of helium flowing from two producers. The same summary puts the estimated 2025 base level for Grade-A helium at about $12 per cubic meter, or $330 per thousand cubic feet [21].

Management’s view of the helium volume is the reason to be careful. It expects the plant to run at about 20% of its 1,200 metric tons next year, not 50%, and says the ramp will be gradual [9]. A plant at a fifth of capacity has a partial revenue line, however strong the market is.

web_blocks.region_era: United States and global, FY2022 to FY2024, refrigerant substitution after the EU Mobile Air Conditioning Directive
web_blocks.mechanism: A regulation forced a change of refrigerant. The company had developed a lower-warming replacement in response to that rule, and its sales moved toward it while the legacy refrigerant line shrank.
web_blocks.outcome_numbers: Opteon refrigerant sales were $597 million in 2022, $710 million in 2023 and $810 million in 2024. Freon refrigerant sales over the same years were $750 million, $722 million and $614 million [27].
web_blocks.lesson_for_symbol: Stallion faces the same kind of change. Its R-32 is an HFC that the treaty caps, so its HFO line has to grow fast enough to replace the volume the cap removes. Watch the HFO plant’s capex and volumes, not the timetable alone.

web_blocks.title: NARRATOR’S REFLECTION
paragraphs: Put the clocks side by side. The freeze arrives on 1 January 2028. The HFO plant, by management’s own timetable, starts construction in 2027 and needs time to produce. Ask yourself what the company sells in the gap between the freeze and the substitute plants running at full output.
The answer depends on the ceiling India sets, which the sources do not give. Until that number is public, treat the timing as the central uncertainty of the regulatory story.

book_paragraphs: Some of the rules that shape this company are not written by the company, or by its auditors, or even by the Indian government alone. They come from a treaty signed decades ago and amended since. The Montreal Protocol began as a way to phase out the gases that damage the ozone layer. The Kigali Amendment, adopted in 2016, brought in a second group of gases, the hydrofluorocarbons, which the company sells as refrigerants. Those gases do not harm the ozone layer, but they trap a lot of heat. So the treaty now limits how much of them the world can make and use, and it does so on a timetable.

The UNEP summary of Kigali says the amendment sets differentiated timelines for developed and developing nations. Developed countries started their reductions in 2019. India sits in a different group. In the HFC annex it is in Group 2, alongside a set of countries in the Gulf and South Asia. For that group the baseline is the average HFC use over 2024 to 2026, plus 65 percent of an older HCFC baseline. From 1 January 2028, the country is frozen at that level. That is the date to put on the wall.

Think about what a freeze does to a refrigerant distributor. It does not stop the business. It caps the total volume the country can consume, and then the question becomes who gets the volume inside that cap. The treaty summary does not answer that, and neither do the company’s filings in the sources I checked. You need the national allocation rule before you can say much about the company’s refrigerant volume after 2028. Until you have it, you are guessing, and you should say you are guessing.

The company’s main product, R-32, is an HFC. The planned Bhilwara plant would make it, so that plant is also inside the freeze. The substitutes are the HFOs, which are lower in warming potential. The company supplies HFO-1234yf to Indian auto makers, and it has an HFO plant planned at Bhilwara under a memorandum of understanding with the state. The annual report puts that plant at about 200 crore, with construction from 2027. Management, on the August call, put the capital cost of the HFO plant much higher, at 350 to 400 crore. Both figures appear to describe the same HFO plant, and the sources do not explain the gap, so do not average them or pick the one you like.

The helium part of the business rests on partners. Liquid helium comes through a partner in Dubai that sources from a producer in Qatar. Helium is recovered as a by-product of other gas production. The company does not own a source. So its helium volume depends on what the producers make, and that is a different risk from the refrigerant regulation. The USGS figures on helium imports are for the United States, not India, and they show that a large share of the world’s helium comes from very few producers. That is useful context. It is not a description of this company’s supply.

Management expects the Khalapur helium plant to run at about 20 percent of its 1,200 metric tons next year, and it expects the ramp to be gradual. That is an honest answer, and it is much lower than the number an analyst put to it. A plant running at a fifth of capacity is a real business, but it is not the full plant. Keep that in mind when you see any helium revenue figure in the coming quarters.

Finally, look at one company outside India that faced a forced change of refrigerant. Chemours, a United States chemical maker, developed a lower-warming replacement called Opteon in response to a European rule on car air conditioners, and its own filing says so. Over three years Opteon sales rose from $597 million to $810 million. Over the same years its older Freon refrigerant sales fell from $750 million to $614 million. The lesson is not that the switch was easy. It is that the replacement was there to take the volume as the old line shrank. Stallion’s HFO plan is the same kind of bet, so the timing of that plant is the test.

Read the treaty as a schedule, not a headline. The Montreal Protocol and its amendments do not say what a given company will sell in a given year. They set a ceiling for the country and a date for the ceiling to bite. Everything the company does after that date sits under the ceiling, so the ceiling is the number to carry into every forecast you read.

Keep two dates on the same page: the freeze on 1 January 2028, and the company’s own plant dates. The freeze arrives about a year after management’s end-December 2026 target for Bhilwara. A plant that starts late gives the company less time to sell into the period before the cap bites, so check the Bhilwara date and the freeze date together.

A regulation is only as firm as the rule that allocates it. The sources I checked do not describe how India will divide its HFC volume after the freeze. You will need the government’s allocation rule, and you will need to know whether it is published before 2028. Until then, the company’s refrigerant volume after 2028 has an open question at its centre, and it is worth asking management about it on each call until someone answers.

book_callouts.title: NARRATOR’S REFLECTION
book_callouts.text: Put the two dates in one line. The freeze comes in 2028, and the substitute plant starts construction in 2027 and needs time to run. What does this company sell in the gap? If you cannot answer that from the filings, write the question down and keep it until the allocation rule is public.
